summary: Ages 9–11 META topic on HOW we explore the ocean and the LIMITS of what we know. Learners (1) match exploration tools (crewed submersible, ROV, sonar, satellite, diver) to the problem each solves; (2) explain why the deep is hard — darkness below ~1000 m, pressure hundreds of times the surface, planet-sized vastness, and radio/light not travelling through deep water; and (3) distinguish three senses of 'explored' — coarsely mapped (~100%), high-resolution mapped (~29%), and directly SEEN (<0.001%) — then critically evaluate the slogan 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' rather than accepting or dismissing it. The peak activity is an in-role dialogue with an ocean explorer who both answers and probes the child's thinking; concrete ROV-sim and tool-matching activities build the factual grounding.
misconceptions: 'We've explored most of the ocean' — vs directly seeing far less than 1% of the deep seafloor.
Uncritically accepting 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' as a current fact — it is outdated and conflates mapping, seeing and understanding.
'Mapped = explored/seen' — conflating a coarse satellite map with direct visual observation.
'Satellites can photograph the deep seafloor' — not knowing light/radio don't penetrate deep water, so sonar/ROVs are needed.
Thinking scientific knowledge is fixed — rather than growing and being revised as tools and evidence improve.

activities.title: Interview an ocean explorer (in-role dialogue)
steps: Interview someone in the role of a deep-sea explorer fresh from a submersible dive: ask what it looks like out the porthole a kilometre down, what happens as pressure rises, and how much of the deep sea has actually been seen.
Respond when the explorer turns a question back: 'People love saying we know more about the Moon than the ocean — is that even true? What do you mean by "know"?'
State, in your own words, the difference between mapping the shape of the seafloor, SEEING it with your own eyes, and UNDERSTANDING it.
Say what evidence you would check (e.g. how much seafloor is mapped at high resolution) before repeating the Moon claim.
activities.insight: 'Explored' has several meanings — coarsely mapped, high-resolution mapped, and directly observed are different; we have directly seen a tiny fraction of the deep seafloor; and the catchy 'more than the Moon' line is an old, contested claim to interrogate, not a fact to store.

activities.title: Pilot an ROV descent and tally what you've seen
steps: Descend a simulated ROV/submersible: manage a limited headlamp cone in the darkness, watch a pressure gauge climb as you go deeper, and use sonar to map a narrow strip of seafloor.
Watch a running bar that shows how little of the vast floor you have covered after a full dive.
Describe afterwards why this makes exploration slow and costly, naming darkness, pressure, and vastness as reasons.
activities.insight: The difficulty of deep-sea exploration becomes concrete: no sunlight, rising pressure, and a planet-sized area mean each dive reveals only a tiny strip, so direct observation of the deep seafloor stays vanishingly small.

activities.title: Match the tool to the job
steps: Match each tool to the problem it solves: ROV = eyes on site without risking people; sonar = mapping shape with sound instead of light; satellite = broad surface view and coarse seafloor mapping worked out indirectly from tiny bumps in sea-surface height; crewed submersible = humans on site; diver = shallow, hands-on work.
Explain why a satellite cannot photograph the deep seafloor and what is used instead.
Place three labels on a 'three kinds of explored' bar: coarsely mapped ~100%, high-resolution mapped ~29%, directly seen <0.001%.
activities.insight: Each instrument extends a different sense and addresses a specific barrier; 'mapped' (especially coarsely) is not the same as 'directly seen', and satellites cannot image the deep because light/radio do not penetrate deep water — their coarse seafloor maps are worked out indirectly from the shape of the sea surface.

activities.title: Check your facts and examine the Moon claim
steps: Match each tool to its job.
Answer multiple-choice items on why deep-sea exploration is hard (darkness, pressure, vastness, light and radio signals not travelling far through water).
Answer an item that distinguishes 'mapped' from 'directly seen'.

Without giving a true/false verdict, say what 'we know more about the Moon than the ocean' would need to compare (high-resolution maps, direct observation or understanding), and why it should be examined rather than simply accepted or rejected.
activities.insight: Factual checks (tools, difficulties, mapped-vs-seen) can confirm the evidence goals, while the Moon item is used to prompt critical examination rather than a simple right/wrong store.

checkQuestion: People often say 'we know more about the surface of the Moon than about the deep ocean floor', even though the ocean is right here on our own planet. What do you think that claim really means — and how could that even be true when the ocean is so much closer to us than the Moon? What would you want to check before you believed it, or repeated it?
checkAnswer: There is no single right answer to score — listen for the QUALITY of the reasoning. Strong responses (a) unpack what the claim actually means (it's about how much of each has been MAPPED/imaged at high resolution and directly observed, not literally 'everything about the Moon'); (b) explain why closeness doesn't equal ease — the deep ocean is dark, crushingly high-pressure, vast and hard to send signals through, so we explore it with submarines, ROVs, satellites and sonar rather than just looking; (c) treat the slogan critically — ask what 'know more' is being measured, notice it's a memorable comparison that can be out of date, and say they'd check a reliable source (how much seafloor is mapped at high resolution) before repeating it. The point is not to accept OR dismiss the slogan, but to interrogate it.
